qs.q: In a patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and a pan-reactive antibody screen who has been recently transfused, which method is best used to detect underlying alloantibodies?
o: Use autologous adsorption for testing the sample.
Perform an acid elution procedure on the red cells.
Use allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells.
Apply the saline replacement technique on the serum.
qs.e: Autologous adsorption cannot be used in recently transfused patients because donor cells would adsorb the alloantibody too. Allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells removes the autoantibody while preserving detectable alloantibodies.

qs.q: In a patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and a pan-reactive antibody screen, which method is used to detect underlying alloantibodies if the patient has been transfused in the last 3 months?
o: Use allogeneic adsorption with matched cells
qs.e: Autologous adsorption can't be used in recently transfused patients (donor cells would adsorb the alloantibody too). Allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells removes the autoantibody while preserving detectable alloantibodies.

qs.q: Most common cause of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
qs.e: About half of warm AIHA cases have no identifiable underlying cause.

es.q: List and explain the rationale for using allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells in a patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and a pan-reactive antibody screen.
es.m:
- Autologous adsorption cannot be used in recently transfused patients.
- In recent transfusion, donor cells would adsorb the alloantibody as well, masking it.
- Allogeneic adsorption uses phenotype-matched cells to remove the autoantibody.
- This method preserves detectable alloantibodies for identification.
- It allows for the detection of underlying alloantibodies in complex WAIHA cases.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with SLE presents with Hb 6 g/dL, jaundice and dark urine. What investigations confirm warm AIHA and why? — DAT positive for IgG, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin; these together prove immune hemolysis.
You receive a transfusion request for a patient with severe WAIHA. Which blood product is safest and why? — Washed, compatible red cells to remove plasma antibodies that could exacerbate hemolysis.
A patient on penicillin develops anemia; DAT is negative. How do you proceed? — Consider drug‑induced non‑immune hemolysis or repeat DAT after 48 h; stop penicillin and monitor.
Explain why renal failure can occur early in warm AIHA. — Massive intravascular hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, which precipitates in renal tubules causing acute tubular necrosis.

In a low‑resource hospital, the DAT machine is broken. What alternative approach helps you diagnose WAIHA? — Rely on clinical picture, peripheral smear showing spherocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, and response to steroids.

A patient with malaria infection now has hemolysis. How do you differentiate malaria‑induced hemolysis from warm AIHA? — Malaria shows parasites on smear, DAT negative; warm AIHA shows positive DAT and spherocytes.

Why is rituximab preferred over splenectomy in many East African settings? — Rituximab avoids surgical risk, preserves splenic immunity, and can be given outpatient where operative facilities are limited.
What red‑flag sign would make you call for urgent dialysis in a WAIHA patient? — Oliguria with rising creatinine and hemoglobinuria indicating severe intravascular hemolysis‑related renal injury.
ai.title: Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) is a IgG‑mediated destruction of red cells that occurs mainly in the spleen but can also cause intravascular hemolysis. It presents with anemia, jaundice and sometimes renal impairment, especially in low‑resource settings where infections and drugs are common triggers.

b: Positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) for IgG ± C3d
Elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin
Reticulocytosis >2 % (or absolute >100 ×10⁹/L)
sections.p: WAIHA is a hemolytic anemia caused by IgG auto‑antibodies that bind red cells at body temperature, leading to opsonisation and splenic clearance; intravascular hemolysis may also occur.

t.b: Does the patient have IgG‑mediated auto‑antibodies? Positive DAT confirms WAIHA; negative DAT suggests other hemolysis.
What is the morphology of red cells? Spherocytes support immune hemolysis; schistocytes suggest mechanical destruction.
Is hemolysis occurring? High indirect bilirubin and LDH with low haptoglobin indicate active hemolysis.
Is the marrow responding? Elevated retic shows compensatory erythropoiesis; low retic suggests marrow failure.
Is there a circulating auto‑antibody? May help identify drug‑induced cases.

b: Mild: Hb ≥ 10 g/dL, no organ dysfunction
Moderate: Hb 7‑9 g/dL, stable, no renal failure
Severe: Hb < 7 g/dL or acute drop > 2 g/dL in 24 h, or renal impairment (creatinine rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL)
sections.p: Severity is gauged by hemoglobin level, rate of fall, and presence of organ dysfunction (renal, cardiac, neurologic).

b: Primary (idiopathic) – 30‑40 % of cases
Secondary infections – HIV, malaria, TB, hepatitis B
Drugs – penicillins, cephalosporins, quinine, herbal preparations
Autoimmune disease – systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis
sections.p: Identify the trigger because treatment hinges on removing it. In East Africa, infections and certain drugs dominate.

b: Pallor, tachycardia, dyspnoea on exertion
Yellow sclerae, dark urine (hemoglobinuria)
Splenomegaly, mild fever
Acute kidney injury: oliguria, rising creatinine
sections.p: Patients often arrive with fatigue, pallor, jaundice and dark urine; splenomegaly is common. In low‑resource settings, renal failure may be the first clue.
Prioritise tests that confirm hemolysis and identify the trigger; adapt when equipment is limited.

t.a: Full blood count with reticulocyte index
t.b: Is there anemia and marrow response? Low Hb with high retic supports hemolysis; if retic is low, consider marrow disease.
Are hemolysis markers abnormal? Elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin with low haptoglobin confirm active destruction.
Is immune hemolysis present? Positive IgG DAT is diagnostic of warm AIHA.
Is there renal involvement? Rising creatinine indicates intravascular hemolysis complications.

t.a: HIV, hepatitis B serology, malaria rapid test
t.b: Is a secondary infection present? Positive result directs specific therapy.
Is a drug trigger likely? Identifying and stopping the offending agent can halt hemolysis.

b: Hb drop > 2 g/dL in 24 h
Acute kidney injury (creatinine rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL)
Severe jaundice with bilirubin > 15 mg/dL
Thromboembolic events – high LDH, hemolysis‑related hypercoagulability
sections.p: Rapid hemoglobin fall, renal failure, and severe hyperbilirubinemia demand urgent action.

b: Discontinue offending drug or herbal product immediately
If no response in 7‑10 days: add rituximab (anti‑CD20) or consider IVIG in emergencies
Transfusion of washed, compatible red cells for severe anemia
Hydration and diuretics to protect kidneys; avoid nephrotoxic drugs
sections.p: First stop the trigger, then suppress antibody production, and finally support the patient’s circulation and kidneys.

b: Weekly CBC and LDH until stable, then monthly for 6 months
Screen for relapse when Hb falls > 1 g/dL or retic rises sharply
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (splenectomy rarely needed)
Counsel on avoiding quinine, penicillins and unregulated herbal remedies
sections.p: Monitor hemoglobin, hemolysis markers and renal function; educate about drug avoidance and infection prophylaxis.

b: Cold agglutinin disease – DAT positive for C3d only, symptoms worsen in cold
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria – flow cytometry shows CD55/CD59 loss, hemoglobinuria nocturnal
G6PD deficiency – bite cells, triggered by oxidative drugs, DAT negative
sections.p: Distinguish WAIHA from other hemolytic processes that share jaundice and anemia.

b: Haptoglobin may be normal if liver synthesis is up‑regulated in chronic disease
DAT can be negative in low‑titer antibodies; repeat if suspicion remains
Serum bilirubin may be normal in early hemolysis; rely on LDH and retic
sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal early or be altered by co‑existing conditions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden Hb drop >2 g/dL in 24 h
Signs of cardiac ischemia or heart failure
